cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-84-christ.summary: To the right the bearded psalmist raises his hand to the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, who appears half-revealed in the heavens with a cross-staff, turning his head back toward him: 'wilt thou not revive us again?'. Angels with cross-staffs spread a cover over a group of the faithful — 'thou hast covered all their sin' — and personifications of the psalm's virtues appear in the heavens at the left. It is a tender image of reconciliation.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-84-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-108-chris.summary: On a mountain top the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos sits in a globe-mandorla among angels, two of whom turn toward a wicked man being seized by a demon below: 'let Satan stand at his right hand'. Opposite, an angel supports the bearded psalmist, 'poor and needy'. Christian readers applied this cursing psalm to Judas, whose office 'another shall take'.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.

The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

feat:rossano-gospels-christ-before-pilat.summary: On a page of purple-dyed parchment, Pontius Pilate sits on his tribunal, flanked by imperial standards bearing portraits of the emperor, while Christ stands calmly before him and the crowd presses in. Painted with the immediacy of a theatre scene, it belongs to one of the oldest surviving illustrated Gospel books in the world. The page sets the dignity of the accused Christ against the machinery of imperial justice.
facts: Purple parchment was associated with imperial luxury, and the Greek text of the manuscript is written in silver and gold ink.
A companion page shows the crowd choosing between Christ and Barabbas, a rare early depiction of that moment.
The manuscript was brought to scholarly attention in 1879 by the German scholars Oscar von Gebhardt and Adolf von Harnack.
In 2015 it was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World register.
